revolutionary-battles-1775-1776.works: Each battle pop-up puts the date in large type right under the title, so a student who can't read the long English story still gets what the sheet asks for. Red and blue diamonds and the two anchor sizes are easy to tell apart, and the Spanish sheet gives the English names in brackets for Key Port Cities, Major Port City, Port, Map layers and Measure.

findings.where: q1-bookmark and q4-circles views; Turning Points drawn over Revolutionary War Battles; Q1 step 4 (Boston diamond) and Q4 steps 3-4 (Fort Washington, Fort Lee, Trenton, who won)
findings.what: The numbered white circles sit right on top of the diamonds my students need. At Boston, circle 2 covers the Boston diamond. Near New York, circle 4 covers the Fort Washington and Fort Lee diamonds and circle 5 covers Trenton. All I can see through the circles is a faint pink or blue tint. Clicking circle 4 gives '1 of 5', and at that zoom there is no blue diamond visible anywhere near New York, even though the legend lists American Victory.
findings.why: The sheet says the diamond's colour is the only way to know who won, because the battle pop-ups don't say it in words. If the colour is hidden, my English learners can't answer 'who won'. Their only way round it is to page through five long English pop-ups and guess which one is which battle.
findings.suggestion: Offset the Turning Points circles from the battle diamonds, for example a little to one side with a short leader line, or draw Turning Points underneath the diamonds. Add a line to each battle pop-up, 'Result: British Victory' or 'Result: American Victory', in exactly the legend's words. Add to both sheets: 'If a circle covers the diamond, use the arrows in the pop-up to find the battle' / 'Si un círculo tapa el rombo, usa las flechas de la ventana para encontrar la batalla.'
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-bookmark.png (circle 2 over Boston); revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q4-circles.png (circles 3, 4, 5 over Brooklyn, Fort Washington/Fort Lee, Trenton; no blue diamond visible); revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q4-circle4.png (pop-up '1 of 5')

findings.where: Map layers list; Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781; Q3 step 1
findings.what: Both sheets say the port layer is inside Revolutionary War Battlefields ('está dentro de Revolutionary War Battlefields'). In the app's Map layers list it is a layer of its own, second from the top. Inside Revolutionary War Battlefields there are only Revolutionary War Core Areas and Revolutionary War Battlefield Boundary.
findings.why: My students match long English layer names letter by letter. If the sheet sends them to the wrong group, they open it, can't find the name, and decide they've done something wrong.
findings.suggestion: Change both sheets, and the From the front step, to 'In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (second in the list)' / '(la segunda de la lista)'. Or move the layer into the Revolutionary War Battlefields group so the map matches the sheet.
findings.evidence: Map layers list as the app lists it: 'Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off)' at top level; the Revolutionary War Battlefields group holds only Core Areas and Battlefield Boundary

findings.where: q3-ports and q3-port views; Key Port Cities layer; Q3 steps 3-4 and Cómo leer el mapa
findings.what: The sheet says the port layer has no pop-ups, and asks students to work out the city names from the coastline and the nearby diamonds. But clicking an anchor opened a pop-up that just says 'Stonington, CT'. The big anchors for New York, Philadelphia and Norfolk have no labels, and at this zoom the basemap shows only colony names.
findings.why: Working out that the anchor up the Delaware is Philadelphia takes US geography my newcomers don't have yet, plus a chain of reasoning in a second language. A pop-up with the city name is exactly the support they need, but the sheet tells them there isn't one, so they won't click.
findings.suggestion: Check that the major-port anchors also open a name pop-up. If they do, change step 4 on both sheets to 'Click each large anchor to read the city's name' / 'Haz clic en cada ancla grande para leer el nombre de la ciudad', and remove 'no tiene ventanas emergentes' from Cómo leer el mapa. Better still, label the five major ports on the map.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q3-port.png, pop-up text 'Stonington, CT'; revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q3-ports.png (major-port anchors with no labels)

findings.where: q2-colony, q2-colony-ny and q2-all views; Thirteen British Colonies; Q2 step 3 (click the colony to read its name)
findings.what: Step 3 says to click the colony to read its name. Clicking inside Virginia opened nothing, and so did clicking inside New York. At the zoom that shows South Carolina, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and New Jersey have no labels. The Boston diamonds sit between the 'New Hampshire' and 'Connecticut' labels, and the Rhode Island diamond is right next to 'Connecticut'. Where 'Massachusetts' does appear, it is up in what is now Maine.
findings.why: My students do exactly what the sheet says. When nothing happens, they copy the nearest name they can see. They'll write Connecticut or New Hampshire for the Boston battles and miss Rhode Island and New Jersey, which the answer needs.
findings.suggestion: Turn on the Thirteen British Colonies pop-up (just the colony name). Or change step 3 on both sheets to 'Zoom in until the colony's name appears' / 'Acércate hasta que aparezca el nombre de la colonia', and make the Massachusetts, Rhode Island and New Jersey labels draw at this zoom, with Massachusetts placed near Boston.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-colony.png and revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-colony-ny.png (no pop-up opened; no Massachusetts, Rhode Island or New Jersey label); revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-colony-ny.png ('Massachusetts' label placed in Maine)

findings.where: q1-lexington pop-up; Revolutionary War Battles; Q1 step 5 (Measure from Boston to Concord)
findings.what: The Lexington and Concord pop-up says Concord is '20 miles northwest of Boston'. The answer notes expect about 16 miles from Measure.
findings.why: When the English is hard, my students hunt for numbers. Some will copy 20 from the pop-up instead of measuring, and others will think Measure is wrong when it gives 16.
findings.suggestion: Change the pop-up to 'about 16 miles (in a straight line) northwest of Boston'. Or add to step 5 on both sheets: 'The pop-up gives the distance by road. Measure gives a straight line.' I'd check which distance the pop-up's source means.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-lexington.png; pop-up text '...stored in Concord, Massachusetts, 20 miles northwest of Boston.'

findings.where: q2-all and q2-colony-ny views; Revolutionary War Battles; Q2 step 1 (zoom out to see every diamond)
findings.what: On a laptop screen with the legend open, the view that shows the South Carolina diamond cuts the Quebec diamond off the top. The view that shows Quebec cuts off North and South Carolina.
findings.why: 'Aléjate hasta ver todos los rombos' is clear Spanish, but students keep zooming in and out trying to fit all 21 on screen. Some stop before they've seen Quebec or South Carolina, and both are in the answer.
findings.suggestion: Add a bookmark called 'All battles 1775-1776' that shows Quebec to Charleston, and point step 1 on both sheets to it.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-all.png (Quebec off the top); revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-colony-ny.png (Quebec shown, Carolinas off the bottom)

findings.where: Bookmarks tool and Turning Points layer; Spanish sheet, Cómo leer el mapa, Q1 step 1 and Q4 steps 1-2
findings.what: The Spanish sheet gives the English names for Map layers and Measure, but it says 'Abre el marcador Massachusetts' without '(Bookmarks)'. It also calls the circles 'cinco momentos decisivos' without ever giving the name 'Turning Points' that the legend and layer list use.
findings.why: 'Marcador' looks nothing like 'Bookmarks', and 'momentos decisivos' looks nothing like 'Turning Points'. Students working from the Spanish can't find the button or match the legend heading.
findings.suggestion: In the Spanish sheet, write 'Abre el marcador (Bookmarks) Massachusetts' and 'círculos blancos numerados (Turning Points): cinco momentos decisivos'.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-bookmark.png, legend heading 'Turning Points'; app tool named Bookmarks

roads-trails-and-rails-west.works: The legend names every trail with the same proper nouns the Spanish sheet uses, and each pop-up's title bar names the trail, so a student can check which one opened. The Spanish sheet gives Railroads, Indigenous Territories and both Transcontinental Railroad names exactly as the map shows them, and the gray railroad pop-up is short, with the year on a line of its own.

findings.where: q2-oregon view; Trails West; Q2 step 2 (click the Oregon Trail and read its length and number of travelers)
findings.what: I clicked the Oregon Trail in Nebraska, where the trails run together, and got 'Pony Express Trail', 1 of 4. That pop-up is full of numbers: 153 stations, 10-15 miles, 2897 kilometers, 1,800 miles, 10 days.
findings.why: My English learners will see a long paragraph with '1,800 miles' in it and write that down as the Oregon Trail's length. The 1-of-4 arrows are small, and the tip about them on the front of the sheet is easy to forget halfway through a task.
findings.suggestion: Draw the Oregon trail on top within Trails West, so its pop-up comes first on the shared stretch. Add to step 2 on both sheets: 'Check that the pop-up title says Oregon Trail; if not, use the arrows' / 'Comprueba que el título dice Oregon Trail; si no, usa las flechas.' Or tell students to click the Oregon line in Idaho or Oregon, where it runs alone.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q2-oregon.png (pop-up 'Pony Express Trail', '1 of 4'); pop-up text 'mail could travel more than 2897 kilometers (1,800 miles) in just 10 days'

findings.where: open and q3-indigenous views; Trails West legend; Q1 step 1, Q2 step 1, Q3 step 3 (follow one trail)
findings.what: The Oregon and California dotted lines are two olive greens that look almost the same. Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish and Pony Express are all very dark dots: near-black, dark brown and dark red. Along the Platte, four of them run on top of each other.
findings.why: Matching a colour to the legend is the one step on this map that needs no English, and here it doesn't work. Students who can't match the colour have to click and read long English pop-ups just to know which trail they're following.
findings.suggestion: Give the seven trails clearly different colours, for example Oregon green, California blue, Mormon Pioneer purple and Pony Express red, and label each trail along its line with its name.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--open.png (legend swatches and trails); roads-trails-and-rails-west--q3-indigenous.png (overlapping dark dotted lines along the Platte)

findings.where: Trails West pop-ups (q2-oregon); Q1 step 3 (where each trail started and ended), Q2 step 2
findings.what: Where each trail starts and ends, how long it is and how many people used it are buried inside long paragraphs. The Pony Express pop-up runs to two paragraphs, and its start and end points are in the middle of the first sentence.
findings.why: For my newer English learners, pulling two place names and a number out of a 150-word paragraph is the hardest part of the lesson, and it isn't the history skill the question is testing.
findings.suggestion: Put four short lines at the top of each trail pop-up, before the story, for example 'Start: St. Joseph, Missouri / End: Sacramento, California / Length: about 1,800 miles / Years used: 1860-1861', with the number of travelers where it is known.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q2-oregon.png; pop-up text 'deliver mail from St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento, California in 10 days...'

findings.where: q3-indigenous view; Indigenous Territories; Q3 steps 2-4 (find two nations whose land the trail crossed)
findings.what: Zoomed in on Wyoming and Nebraska, the nation names are in the same small gray type as the town names: 'Tsėhéstȯhe (Cheyenne)', 'Oohenumpa', 'Sicangu', 'Pa'ka'to'de'uk'ethi' (Ponca)'. Just below them is the town of 'Cheyenne'. The shaded areas overlap and blend their colours, and the two areas the trail actually crosses in this view have no name on them.
findings.why: My students can't tell a nation's name from a town's. They'll happily write 'Cheyenne' from the town label, and they won't know how to copy names with letters like ė and ȯ. They also can't tell which label belongs to which shaded area.
findings.suggestion: Label the territories in a style that's clearly different from the basemap, for example larger italic text with a white halo, centred in each area. Give the common English name in brackets for every nation, as is already done for Cheyenne and Ponca. On both sheets, say how to tell nation names from town names.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q3-indigenous.png (labels 'Tsėhéstȯhe (Cheyenne)', 'Oohenumpa', 'Sicangu' next to the town label 'Cheyenne'; unlabeled overlapping areas under the trail)

findings.where: q4-railroads view; Railroads 1826 to 1911 and the Transcontinental Railroads legend; Q4 steps 1-2
findings.what: The sheets say 'thin gray lines' / 'líneas grises finas'. Zoomed out, the lines look black, and east of the Mississippi they are so dense that they hide the eastern ends of the trails. With the legend open, the list is cut off at 'Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific)', and Southern Pacific only shows if you scroll.
findings.why: Small mismatches like gray against black make my students doubt they've turned on the right layer, and the line they're told to find in the legend is half hidden.
findings.suggestion: Draw Railroads 1826 to 1911 thinner and lighter gray when zoomed out, or change the sheets to 'thin dark lines'. Add to step 2: 'Scroll down in the legend' / 'Baja en la leyenda'.
findings.evidence: roads-trails-and-rails-west--q4-railroads.png

us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850.works: Each state pop-up is titled with the state's name and gives the year in its first sentence, and the brown/green split and the solid black trade routes read clearly at the opening view. At the bookmark, the orange routes with orange town dots and labels are easy to follow without much English.

findings.where: q2-line view; Missouri Compromise Line; Q2 step 2 (click the line and read its pop-up)
findings.what: Clicking the gray dashed line opened the pop-up for 'Unorganized Territory', the area just north of it. There were no 1-of-2 arrows, so the line's own pop-up never appeared.
findings.why: The sheet says to click the line and read its pop-up. My students get a title that doesn't match, may copy 1820 by luck, and miss the note that Missouri is the exception, which is the whole point of the question.
findings.suggestion: Make the Missouri Compromise Line's pop-up come before the states layer's: keep the line on top and give it a wider click area. Or label the line on the map: 'Missouri Compromise Line, 36°30′ N, 1820'.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q2-line.png; pop-up text 'Unorganized Territory ... in 1820 ... Free by Missouri Compromise'

findings.where: q1-pennsylvania pop-up; US States and Territories 1850; Q1 step 3 (read what year each state became free or slave)
findings.what: Pennsylvania's pop-up first says 'passed legislation against the enslavement of people 1780' and then 'Abolition by state action between 1830-1850'.
findings.why: There are two different dates in one short pop-up, and several of my students will write down 1830-1850. The missing 'in' before 1780 makes the first sentence harder to parse.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite the first line in plain English: 'Pennsylvania passed a law to end slavery in 1780.' Introduce the second as 'Group on the 1920 map: Abolition by state action between 1830-1850', so it reads as a category, not a year. Check the other free states for the same clash.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q1-pennsylvania.png; pop-up text 'This state passed legislation against the enslavement of people 1780. ... Abolition by state action between 1830-1850'

findings.where: Legend, US States and Territories 1850; Spanish sheet, Q1 steps 1-2 and Answer; Q4 step 1
findings.what: The legend headings are 'Free states', 'Free states and territories by compromise', 'Slave states' and 'Slave states and territories by compromise'. Each is followed by a long line such as 'Slave state by annexation, Compromise of 1850, by old French law'. The Spanish sheet talks about 'libres' and 'esclavistas' but never gives the English headings, and it says 'marcador' without '(Bookmarks)'.
findings.why: 'Free' looks nothing like 'libre', so my students can't link the Spanish question to the legend. The long legend lines are the densest English on the map, and the answer doesn't need them.
findings.suggestion: In Cómo leer el mapa on the Spanish sheet, list the four headings with translations: Free states (estados libres); Free states and territories by compromise (libres por un compromiso); Slave states (estados esclavistas); Slave states and territories by compromise (esclavistas por un compromiso). Also write 'marcador (Bookmarks)'. On the map, consider shortening the legend lines and moving the detail into the pop-ups.
findings.evidence: Legend text for us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--open.png and --q3-slavetrade.png

findings.where: q4-bookmark view; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes and Cities; Q4 steps 1-3 (where do the routes lead)
findings.what: The Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark stops at Lake Erie. With the legend open, the only black Canadian dot (Chatham) sits at the edge of the panel with its label cut to 'Cha', and Toronto and Montreal are off the screen.
findings.why: The answer is that the routes lead to Canada. My students follow the orange lines to the lake and stop. They never see the black dots that the legend calls 'Canada', so they can't answer 'why keep going past the free states' from the map.
findings.suggestion: Widen the bookmark to the north-east to take in southern Ontario (Chatham and Toronto), or add a second bookmark for Ontario and Quebec. Add a step to both sheets: 'Follow the routes across the lake to the black dots (Canada)' / 'Sigue las rutas al otro lado del lago hasta los puntos negros (Canadá)'.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q4-bookmark.png (Chatham dot at the panel edge, label cut off; Toronto and Montreal not in view)

findings.where: open and q3-slavetrade views; legend panel over US States and Territories 1850; Q1 Answer (where is the line between free and slave states in the East)
findings.what: In the opening view, with the legend open as Q1 step 1 says, the panel covers the East Coast from Maryland north, and Pennsylvania is half hidden.
findings.why: Students looking for the free/slave line in the East can't see it until they close the legend or pan the map, and most won't think to do either.
findings.suggestion: Add a step to Q1 on both sheets: 'Open the Pennsylvania and New England bookmark to see the line in the East' / 'Abre el marcador (Bookmarks) Pennsylvania and New England'. The bookmark already exists.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--open.png; us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q3-slavetrade.png

findings.where: q4-bookmark and q2-line views; Cities labels over basemap labels; Q4 step 3 (read the town names)
findings.what: Several big towns have two labels, an orange one from Cities and a gray one from the basemap, slightly offset: Chicago, Detroit, Indianapolis, Cincinnati, St. Louis. The orange text also sits on orange routes over the brown free-state shading.
findings.why: Doubled, overlapping text is harder for my students to read and copy correctly.
findings.suggestion: Use a basemap without place labels, or give the orange Cities labels a white halo.
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q4-bookmark.png; us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q2-line.png

findings.where: Legend, Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade; Reading the map / Cómo leer el mapa
findings.what: The legend says 'Route of L'Amistead', but the sheets say 'the Amistad' / 'el Amistad'.
findings.why: My Spanish speakers know that 'La Amistad' means friendship. The legend's spelling looks like a different ship, so they won't connect the two.
findings.suggestion: Change the legend label to 'Route of La Amistad'. I'd check the spelling on the 1920 source map, but the ship's name was La Amistad.
findings.evidence: Legend text 'Route of L'Amistead' (us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--open.png)

civil-war-battlefields.works: State names are written on the map, and the blue/brown split between Union and Confederacy is clear in the opening view, so the first question can be done mostly by looking. The Spanish sheet gives the legend words Inconclusive and Other, and the diamond pop-ups are short.

findings.where: q3-railroads view (also q2-dc); Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static); Q3 steps 2-3 (compare the railroads north and south of the boundary)
findings.what: With the states layer off and the map showing Virginia, North Carolina, Kentucky and Tennessee, I can't see a single railroad line, only the basemap, rivers and diamonds. The lines show up only much closer in, as in the Antietam view.
findings.why: The question asks students to compare north and south of the boundary. At a zoom where both sides fit, there's nothing to compare. Zoomed in far enough to see the lines, they see a small patch of one side. No student, English learner or not, can answer this from the map as it is.
findings.suggestion: Change the railroad layer's visibility range so it draws at the regional view, with both sides of the boundary visible from the Atlantic to the Mississippi. Or add a bookmark at the widest zoom where it does draw, and put 'zoom in until the railroads appear' / 'acércate hasta que aparezcan los ferrocarriles' on both sheets.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q3-railroads.png (no railroad lines); civil-war-battlefields--q2-dc.png (none); civil-war-battlefields--q4-diamond.png (dark railroad lines appear at the closer zoom)

findings.where: q3-railroads view; Boundary between Union and Confederacy; Q3 steps 1-3
findings.what: Once the states layer is off, the boundary is faint white dashes on a cream basemap, and every state name disappears along with the layer.
findings.why: My students lose both of their landmarks at once. They can't find the line the sheet tells them to compare across, and there are no names to show them where they are.
findings.suggestion: Give the boundary line a dark outline or halo so it shows on the plain basemap. Instead of switching the states layer off, have students raise its transparency, or keep the state labels in a separate layer that stays on.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q3-railroads.png

findings.where: q2-dc view; U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) labels; Q2 steps 1-3
findings.what: Zoomed in on the capital, the map says 'District of Columbia', not 'Washington, D.C.', and Maryland has no label at all. Pennsylvania, Ohio, West Virginia, Virginia, Delaware and New Jersey are labeled. The states layer has no pop-up, so clicking doesn't help.
findings.why: Both sheets say Washington, D.C., and my students won't know that it's the 'District of Columbia'. And the one state the question is about has no name on the map.
findings.suggestion: Make sure the Maryland label draws at this zoom (the diamonds may be crowding it out), and label the capital 'Washington, D.C. (District of Columbia)'. Or add to both sheets: 'Washington, D.C. is labeled District of Columbia on the map' / 'En el mapa, Washington D. C. aparece como District of Columbia'.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q2-dc.png

findings.where: q4-diamond, q4-gettysburg and q2-dc views; Civil War Battlefield Boundary and Core Areas; Q4 step 2, Reading the map / Cómo leer el mapa
findings.what: On screen the battlefield areas are pale gray-beige: nearly white on the tan Confederate states and pale gray on the blue Union states. In Virginia they look like roads. The English sheet calls them 'tan', the same word you'd use for Virginia's own shade. The Spanish sheet says 'color canela', which my students picture as cinnamon brown, the colour of the Confederate states.
findings.why: Students reading the Spanish will click the brown state shading when they're looking for a battlefield. The key colour word doesn't match what's on the screen.
findings.suggestion: Change the Spanish to 'zonas de color beige claro' and the English to 'pale beige areas', or give the battlefield areas their own outline colour so they stand out against both state shades. Add that you have to zoom in close to see them.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q4-diamond.png; civil-war-battlefields--q4-gettysburg.png; civil-war-battlefields--q2-dc.png

findings.where: open and q2-dc views; legend panel; Q1 step 1, Q2 step 3
findings.what: On a laptop screen, the legend panel shows Civil War Battlefields and the casualty sizes. The five state groups for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) are below the bottom of the panel, cut off at the heading.
findings.why: My students open the legend, see diamonds and numbers, and think that's all there is. Nothing tells them to scroll inside the panel.
findings.suggestion: Move U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) to the top of the legend, or make the casualty key smaller. Add to both sheets: 'Scroll down in the legend' / 'Baja en la leyenda'.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--open.png (heading cut off at the bottom of the panel); civil-war-battlefields--q2-dc.png

findings.where: Legend, U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863); Spanish sheet, Q1 and Q2 Answer
findings.what: The Spanish questions say 'dejaron la Unión antes del ataque' and 'estados fronterizos'. The legend says 'Slave state seceding before Fort Sumter, April 1861' and 'Union slave state (border state)'. The Spanish sheet never gives those English words.
findings.why: 'Seceding' and 'border state' are the key words for the first half of the lesson. 'Fronterizo' doesn't look like 'border', and the Spanish never uses 'secesión', the cognate that would help students recognise 'seceding'.
findings.suggestion: Add a short word box to the Spanish sheet: seceding = separarse (secesión); border state = estado fronterizo; Union Free State = estado libre de la Unión; Territories = territorios.
findings.evidence: Legend text for civil-war-battlefields--open.png

findings.where: Legend, Total casualties; Reading the map ('Bigger diamonds mean more soldiers...')
findings.what: The smallest size in the casualty legend reads '< 0'.
findings.why: Fewer than zero casualties makes no sense. My students who are strong in maths will stop and puzzle over it, and it makes the size key harder to trust.
findings.suggestion: Relabel the smallest class with its real range. I'd check the class breaks in the layer's size settings.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--open.png, legend '< 0'

findings.where: q4-gettysburg and q4-diamond pop-ups; Civil War Battlefield Boundary and Civil War Battlefields; Q4 steps 2-3
findings.what: The Gettysburg pop-up is partly in capitals ('GETTYSBURG', 'CIVIL WAR') and doesn't name the state. The Antietam diamond pop-up repeats 'Antietam', shows a broken image link labeled 'American Battlefield Trust', and gives the dates in small light-gray italics.
findings.why: Words in all capitals and pale italic dates are harder for English learners to read. A state name in the battlefield pop-up would let them answer 'a battle in a Union state' without having to decode the shading.
findings.suggestion: Use normal capitalisation in the battlefield pop-up and add 'State: Pennsylvania' (full name, not the two-letter code). In the diamond pop-up, remove the repeated name, fix or remove the image, and set the dates in plain dark text.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q4-gettysburg.png (pop-up 'The battlefield area in the Battle of GETTYSBURG during the CIVIL WAR'); civil-war-battlefields--q4-diamond.png

the-battle-of-vicksburg.works: The opening view shows all five route pins with bold labels, the yellow Vicksburg pin, the river and the railroad to Jackson in one picture, which is ideal for students who work from the map more than the text. Battle pop-ups are short, with the name and dates at the top, and the Spanish sheet gives the layer and bookmark names in English.

findings.where: q1-bookmark view compared with the open view; Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg; Q1 steps 1-4, Q2 step 1
findings.what: The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark zooms in too far. Milliken's Bend, Edwards and Jackson are off the screen, and the Bruinsburg Bend pin is at the bottom edge with its label hidden. The map as it first opens shows all five pins, Vicksburg, the railroad and Jackson together.
findings.why: Step 1 sends my students to the bookmark, and steps 3-4 and Q2 then ask for places that aren't on the screen. They'll think the pins are missing.
findings.suggestion: Reset the bookmark to the opening view, with all five pins and Jackson in sight. In the Spanish sheet, write 'marcador (Bookmarks)' so students can find the button.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q1-bookmark.png; the-battle-of-vicksburg--open.png

findings.where: q3-battles and q3-championhill views; Civil War Battlefields legend; Q3 steps 1-3, Q4 step 2
findings.what: In this map, Confederate Victory is a gray diamond and Other is a gray circle, which look almost the same at this size. Inconclusive is yellow, the same yellow as the Vicksburg pin. In the Civil War Battlefields lesson, the same layer name used brown for Confederate victories and white for inconclusive.
findings.why: My students have only just learned that brown means Confederate, and they'll read Grand Gulf's gray diamond as 'Other'. A yellow diamond near the yellow pin will be taken for Vicksburg itself.
findings.suggestion: Use the same symbols as the Civil War Battlefields map (brown for Confederate Victory, white for Inconclusive). At the very least, give Confederate Victory its own colour and make Inconclusive any colour other than the pin's yellow.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-battles.png (legend and gray Grand Gulf diamond); civil-war-battlefields--open.png (same layer name, different colours)

findings.where: q4-porthudson view; basemap state names; Q4 steps 1 and 4 (read the state names west of the river)
findings.what: In the zoomed-out view with Port Hudson, I can read 'Alabama', but there's no Louisiana, Texas or Arkansas label, and Memphis is off the top of the screen.
findings.why: Step 4 says to read the state names on the basemap. My students can't find them, and they may not know that Shreveport and Houston are in those states.
findings.suggestion: Add a bookmark 'Mississippi River, Memphis to the Gulf' at a zoom where the basemap draws state names, and check that Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas appear there. Otherwise, add a layer of state-name labels.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q4-porthudson.png

findings.where: q3-championhill and q4-porthudson pop-ups; Civil War Battlefields; Q3 steps 2-3, Q4 step 3
findings.what: Every battle pop-up shows a broken image link, 'Battlefield Trust page', and the words 'Tap on image to view page', but there's no image to tap. The dates are in small light-gray italics.
findings.why: My students try to follow every instruction they read. 'Tap on image' with nothing there sends them clicking around, and the dates, the one thing they need, are the hardest text in the pop-up to read.
findings.suggestion: Fix or remove the image and its caption, and set the date line in plain dark text.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-championhill.png; the-battle-of-vicksburg--q4-porthudson.png; pop-up text 'Battlefield Trust page / Tap on image to view page'

findings.where: open view; Key Places pin labels; Q2 step 1
findings.what: The pin label reads 'Miliken's Bend', with one l, but both sheets say 'Milliken's Bend'. The label also overlaps the basemap's 'Tallulah'.
findings.why: Students who match names letter by letter may think it's a different place.
findings.suggestion: Correct the pin label to 'Milliken's Bend' and move it clear of 'Tallulah'.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--open.png

findings.where: open and q1-bookmark views; Railroads 1826 to 1911 legend; Q1 step 3 (follow the railroad east from Vicksburg)
findings.what: The legend lists Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific), Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Southern Pacific and Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific), and none of them is anywhere near Vicksburg. The line students need is 'others', a light gray line with tick marks, and at the bookmark zoom it's hard to tell apart from Highway 80 and I-20.
findings.why: My students will see 'Southern' in the legend and think it's the Confederacy's railroad. Meanwhile the line they actually need is the faintest thing in the legend.
findings.suggestion: Show a single legend entry, 'Railroads', on this map and draw the lines darker, so they match the sheet's 'thin dark lines with short cross marks'.
findings.evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--open.png and the-battle-of-vicksburg--q1-bookmark.png (legend and railroad line beside the highways)
